text: X flips bits. Z flips a sign. S and T are finer-grained still: they rotate the ket-one amplitude through a specific angle in the complex plane without ever moving it off the ket-one axis. They're called phase gates for a reason, and that name is the whole lesson.

Both gates are diagonal: S is 1, 0, 0, i — a 90-degree rotation of ket-one's amplitude. T is 1, 0, 0, e to the i pi over 4 — a 45-degree rotation. S on ket-one gives i times ket-one, and since the magnitude of i squared is 1, the measurement probability for outcome 1 stays exactly 1, unchanged. S moved the amplitude around the unit circle; it never changed its distance from the origin, and measurement only cares about that distance squared.

The algebra connecting these gates is worth having cold: S squared equals Z, T squared equals S, T to the fourth equals Z, and T to the eighth equals the identity, each confirmed by direct matrix multiplication. Z is a half-turn, S a quarter-turn, T an eighth-turn. Applied alone to a basis state, neither S nor T does anything a measurement could detect — their effect only becomes visible once the qubit is first put into superposition by something like H.

That eighth-turn property is exactly why T matters: a gate set built from just H and T, plus CNOT for multi-qubit work, can approximate any single-qubit rotation to arbitrary precision, because repeated T rotations can land arbitrarily close to any angle. Chapter 4's discussion of universal gate sets depends on exactly this property, and it's why phase gates are never used in isolation in a real circuit.
Next lesson introduces rotation gates — continuous families parameterized by an angle theta, where the fixed gates you already know turn out to be special cases hiding inside them.
